title: Consecration to Mary
hookLine: John Paul II's motto was totally yours, from Montfort

lines: A NEARLY EMPTY COAT OF ARMS.
A CROSS, AND AN M BENEATH IT.
cards: Bishops' coats of arms can get crowded: keys, lions, towers, a shell or two. When Karol Wojtyła became a bishop in Poland, his was nearly empty. A plain cross, a little off center.
Beneath one arm of it, a capital M, for Mary, standing near the cross the way she stood near it on Calvary. And under the shield, two Latin words.
He kept them when he became Pope John Paul the Second, under the same plain cross. Today's word is those two words.

teach.b: First, the words. Totus tuus: totally yours. They're spoken to Mary, but they're not about her alone.
Second, where he found them. You met Louis de Montfort earlier on this path: a French priest who wrote a book on what he called true devotion to Mary.
Its center is an act Catholics call consecration: giving yourself entirely to Jesus, through Mary. Your prayers, your work, your days, all handed to her, so she can bring them to her son.
Totus tuus comes out of that tradition.
John Paul wrote that as a young man he had worried that loving Mary too much might crowd out Christ. Reading Montfort changed his mind.
Devotion to Mary, done rightly, doesn't stop at her; it leads to Christ, the way a mother takes your hand and walks you to her son. Fourth, where it ends.
Paul, writing to the Galatians, describes a life handed over so completely that it's no longer only his own.
In the Douay-Rheims: "And I live, now not I; but Christ liveth in me." Consecration, in this tradition, aims there: Mary is the way in, and her son is the one it reaches.
This week went to the places where Catholics remember her coming, from a spring at Lourdes to a forest at La Vang. Today it stays home, with two words a pope wore under a cross.

how: Some Catholics make a consecration to Jesus through Mary, often following Louis de Montfort's method of preparation, and some renew it each year; Pope John Paul II took Totus Tuus, from this tradition, as his motto.

o: Latin for totally yours, John Paul's motto
Latin for to Jesus through Mary, Montfort's book
Latin for all of you, a greeting at Mass

p: the M on the coat of arms
now not I; but Christ liveth in me

s: John Paul II invented the phrase totus tuus
he took it from the tradition of Louis de Montfort, the French priest who taught consecration to Jesus through Mary.
in Montfort's consecration, the gift ends with Mary
it is a giving of oneself to Jesus, through Mary. she brings it to her son.
Paul writes of a life so handed over that Christ lives in him
Galatians 2:20: "and I live, now not I; but Christ liveth in me."

games.q: you're a young man who loves Christ, and you worry that devotion to Mary might crowd him out. what do you do?
o: drop Marian devotion to be safe.
read Montfort, and give yourself to Jesus through Mary.
keep Mary and Jesus in separate corners of your prayer.
games.why: John Paul II wrote that he had that worry, and that Montfort answered it: devotion to Mary, done rightly, leads to Christ. he took totus tuus as his motto.

practice: Walk through today in your mind, or tomorrow if today is nearly done: the first thing you'll do, the people you'll see, the job you're dreading, the tired end of it, and don't fix any of it.

Then hand the whole day over, the way you'd hand a child to someone you trust. If you pray, say a Hail Mary and the motto's two words, totus tuus; if not, simply hold the day loosely, as something given.

wordCard.voice: Totus Tuus. Latin for totally yours: John Paul the Second's motto, taken from Montfort's consecration of oneself to Jesus through Mary. Today's word, and the end of this week.

orig.note: Latin: totally yours. both words agree with the one speaking, a man; a woman would say tota tua.

carryVoice: Your line: totally yours. Given to her, and reaching him. One thousand three hundred fifty-one days now.
